item.title: Christmas at Noosa Civic
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: There’s something special about the lead-up to Christmas. It’s a season of community, generosity and creating memorable moments with family […]
item.content:encoded:
There’s something special about the lead-up to Christmas. It’s a season of community, generosity and creating memorable moments with family and friends, and Noosa Civic is embracing all of it this year with a month of festive experiences for visitors of all ages.

Adding to the Christmas atmosphere will be live performances from local schools and young musicians, bringing festive favourites and plenty of holiday spirit to the centre. Students from Good Shepherd Lutheran College, St Teresa’s Catholic College and Tewantin State School, along with performers from Eumundi School of Rock, will showcase their talents with performances taking place on 25th, 28th and 30th November, and 1st December.

For many families, a visit to Santa is one of the most magical Christmas traditions, where children can share their wish lists while a festive keepsake photo makes a perfect gift or memory of the year. Dedicated Sensitive Santa and Santa Paws sessions are also available by booking in advance, to ensure everyone can be part of the celebrations.

The season is also a time for giving back. Visitors can lend their support to a range of worthwhile causes through the centre’s gift-wrapping service, with donations benefiting local charities including Rotary Noosa Daybreak, Cancer Council, Australian Red Cross, KNGO and Waves of Kindness. Plus, the SunnyKids Gift Appeal also returns, providing an opportunity for the community to drop a gift in centre to be passed onto vulnerable children and families across the region.

Whether you’re searching for the perfect gift, enjoying the festive entertainment or simply soaking up the holiday atmosphere, Noosa Civic is bringing it all together to celebrate everything that makes this time of year so special.

item.title: I remember Burton
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: On Saturday morning we gathered again on Noosa’s Main Beach to give some of our less fortunate young children a […]
item.content:encoded:
On Saturday morning we gathered again on Noosa’s Main Beach to give some of our less fortunate young children a day at the beach and in the surf. Despite the rain and overcast conditions, about 25 Seahorse Nippers had fun.

As usual, qualified volunteer lifesavers from Noosa Heads, Sunshine Beach and Peregian SLSC provided water safety, and the Sunshine Beach Surf Club bus provided transport to Main Beach. The Bus Boys, Big Pete, Ken and Greg, were on duty again. However, the bus pick-up has moved from Lions Park to the J car park, for a 6:30am service.

This Saturday morning was a sad occasion for me. As I watched the young ones, some of them at the start of their lifesaving careers, I was reminded of my own early days and the guidance I received from a senior Life Member, Burton “Bertie” Hayter.

For some reason, Bertie took me under his wing and told me in no uncertain terms, which direction to take (in 1958) soon as I earned my bronze medallion. In the glove box of his car was a training manual, covering every aspect of surf club life: beach patrolling, upkeep of gear and equipment, and how to run a surf club carnival.

“That, Laney, is the direction you have to take,” he said. “Learn the game and how it’s played, from rescue work to competition – top to bottom.” To be a young clubbie and having a life Member take you under his arm-you couldn’t ask for a better start in your career.”

Now on the afternoon of Friday 4 December, 2pm old boys and Life Members will gather at Easts Leagues Club Brisbane to say a sad farewell: but for me it will be a big- thanks mate, thanks a million. The importance of a rookie learning the ropes (in a rescue organisation from a veteran) was of the utmost importance and could not be emphasised enough. My club mate my mentor. Via Con Dios Bertie, Via Con Dios.

Boxing.

Supporters of Impact Boxing Club (Cooroy) attended the recent Matrix Boxing Tournament, where Theo Rivera, trained by Mark Evans, fought his 23rd bout against Zach Young of Empire Boxing, a very worthy, tough and durable opponent.

From the opening bell it was obvious that both boys came to do business- however Theo marginally edging his way to take round one. Next round saw Zac come out with even more intensity, hoping to put more pressure on Theo and draw him into a full-on slug fest.

It was expected to be a tough contest, but Theo’s determination earned him a well-deserved victory- as his fitness once again gave him the edge. He will glove up once more in Brisbane in November, his final outing of the year and the last hit-out for Team Impact in 2026.

“I am incredibly proud of this young man. As the current Australian Champion, Theo continues to grow from strength to strength with every outing. His experience, fitness, determination and willingness to take on tough opponents, are all contributing to his development as a boxer: 2027 is shaping up to be a massive year for one of Impact’ shining young guns. A superstar in the making!” Another local champion under the coaching and training of the Evans team on the way to better things.

“A massive thank you to all our sponsors for their continued support. Your contribution helps make opportunities like these possible for our athletes. And a special thank you to Kylie Evans, for her continued support, not only of me as a coach, but of every fighter who pulls on the Impact Colours. Your support never goes unnoticed. So, on behalf of Kylie and myself – thank you all. “Team Impact- Stronger Together.

item.title: Beth debuts in Kosci100
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: A host of the top trail runners from across the Asia-Pacific region including Noosa’s Beth McKenzie, will tackle the alpine […]
item.content:encoded:
A host of the top trail runners from across the Asia-Pacific region including Noosa’s Beth McKenzie, will tackle the alpine trails of Ultra-Trail Kosciuszko by UTMB this week with titles across four distances – 30km, 50km, 100km, and 100 miles – on the line.

The event, held from 26-28 November in the Snowy Mountains, NSW, is part of the UTMB World Series and offers the top three female and male finishers in the Kosci50, Kosci100 and KosciMiler the opportunity to earn direct qualification to the 2027 UTMB World Series Finals.

Wearing the number one bib, Mike Carroll will once again headline the men’s KosciMiler. Carroll’s main challenger will likely come in the shape of Christopher McAuliffe, with his compatriot having finished third in the Miler at the 2025 Ultra-Trail Australia by UTMB.

In the women’s KosciMiler, Christie Lori will travel from Perth aiming to build her on her second-place finish from last year, while New Zealand’s Emma Timmis will make the trip across the Tasman hoping to add to her run of four podiums out of the five 100-mile races she’s completed.

In the Kosci100, Adelaide’s former professional cyclist turned trail runner Godfrey Slattery will hope to build on his standout performance from last year, when he finished second just 12 months after swapping two wheels for two feet.

Noosa-based American Beth McKenzie is the top ranked runner in the Kosci100 women’s field and will make her long awaited Ultra-Trail Kosciuszko by UTMB debut.

“I’ve wanted to race in the Snowies for a while,” said McKenzie. “I love that on a new course you get to discover what’s around the next corner on race day. I love that the UTMB events always bring out the best competition in Oceania.”

McKenzie has racked up a string of wins and podiums over the past few years, with notable highlights including her 2024 victory and two runner-up finishes in the 100km race at Ultra-Trail Australia by UTMB and two podiums in the 102km race at Tarawera Ultra-Trail by UTMB.

“I love runnable trails where I can settle into a rhythm, which is something I’ve always enjoyed about Tarawera. Kosci looks like it’ll give me more chances to do that than UTA,” she said.

Now back to full health following a three-week injury setback, McKenzie has enjoyed returning to her long runs and rediscovering the all-day rhythm that comes with them. Heading into Friday, her focus is on staying disciplined with her race plan and making sure she still has plenty to give when it matters most.

“I’m excited to see what I can do with it on Friday. I had a three-week injury hiccup with no running, just five to eight weeks out, but I focused on what I could do and am now back and healthy,” she said. “I want to get to 80km and still feel like I’m racing. If I can do that and give it everything I have from there, I’ll be pretty happy.”

She’ll face a strong contingent of Australian runners including 2025 Kosci100 podium finishers Anna Pillinger and Charlotte Lomas.

The Kosci100 will get underway from 7.30am on Friday, with runners making their way from Perisher to Thredbo. The KosciMiler will start at 3am the same day, beginning in Jindabyne before guiding runners across 160km of trail running wonderland into Thredbo. Both the Kosci100 and KosciMiler courses take runners to the highest point in mainland Australia – Mt Kosciuszko.

item.title: Preparations for disaster
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Noosa disaster management teams are joining police, emergency services and Sunshine Coast Council representatives in a major exercise testing the […]
item.content:encoded:
Noosa disaster management teams are joining police, emergency services and Sunshine Coast Council representatives in a major exercise testing the region’s readiness for the upcoming disaster season.

The exercise, being held today (Tuesday, November 24), will test how agencies respond to two fictional emergencies unfolding simultaneously across the Sunshine Coast and Noosa local government areas.

The scenarios involve multiple bushfires threatening community infrastructure across both regions and an outbreak of avian influenza near a major commercial poultry producer.

The exercise is designed to test disaster management plans, decision-making processes and the ability of agencies to coordinate resources and support when emergencies place competing demands on the region.

Noosa Mayor Frank Wilkie said the simulation was an important opportunity to prepare agencies before disaster struck.

“It’s important to get the right people in the room to test our decision-making processes and ensure we’re ready to respond when needed,” Cr Wilkie said.

“As we regularly tell our residents, preparation is the most important thing during the active storm season and this exercise helps build confidence that we can respond, quickly, effectively and in a coordinated way.”

Sunshine Coast police are working alongside representatives from Noosa Shire Council, Sunshine Coast Council, utility agencies, community support services and other emergency services through the Sunshine Coast District Disaster Management Group.

District Disaster Coordinator Acting Superintendent Craig Mansfield said the exercise had been developed using scientific advice to create a complex training environment.

“The simulation will see potential competing requirements to challenge how we work together with external stakeholders to achieve our objectives,” he said.

“These exercises are vital in ensuring we identify our key priorities at local, district, and state levels and how we get additional help when needed.”

Sunshine Coast Mayor Rosanna Natoli, who chairs the Local Disaster Management Group, said councils needed to be ready to lead communities through emergencies ranging from bushfires, storms and floods to complex biosecurity events.

“We can’t predict what emergencies may unfold this summer, but we can be prepared,” Mayor Natoli said.

“Exercises like this ensure councils, emergency services and government agencies are ready to work together as one team and support our communities when it matters most.”

Disaster management teams, led by local councils and police, have continued preparations to strengthen community resilience ahead of the summer season.

The Queensland Government’s Get Ready activities were launched in October, with today’s exercise another part of the effort to prepare and protect communities.

Residents can find disaster preparation advice at getready.qld.gov.au.

During an emergency, Noosa residents should monitor the Noosa Council disaster dashboard at disaster.noosa.qld.gov.au for current information and warnings.

For life-threatening emergencies, phone Triple Zero (000). For non-life-threatening storm damage and assistance, contact the SES on 132 500.

For the latest weather warnings, visit the Bureau of Meteorology’s Queensland Warnings Summary.

item.title: Community connection and variety of housing needed
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: The nature of community forums is to share knowledge, understand multiple perspectives on an issue, and provide an opportunity for […]
item.content:encoded:
The nature of community forums is to share knowledge, understand multiple perspectives on an issue, and provide an opportunity for a broader community to learn and contribute to important issues affecting them.

This year’s Sunshine Coast Open House community forum at Noosa Arts in Noosaville brought together four of the most passionate and committed individuals who have all made enormous personal sacrifices as well as contributed endless hours to attempt to shape a better future for community housing and human experiences for those engaging in public places.

With the theme Designing Better for Everyone, panelists comprised City of Ryde’s Cr Tina Kordrostami, highly-awarded architect John Mainwaring, founder of Lifestyle Supports disability organisation and registered NDIS service provider Omar Suleiman, and Christopher Kerrisk – a co-founder of verified inclusive venue accessibility platform Cérge

Moderator of the panel was Dr Melissa Innes from University of the Sunshine Coast.

“The stories shared by each panelist highlighted the sometimes confronting and other times inspiring situations faced by every-day Australians managing challenging aspects of a diverse human nature,” Ms Innes said.

“The extraordinary length that each went to – to extend their own unique experience and expertise in an attempt to influence policy around supporting those in the community who perhaps need it most – was phenomenal.

“Ultimately the forum arrived at acknowledging the frustration that our current political system, shaped by often isolated community members acting in self-interest, exacerbates a lack of education and awareness regarding potential building and design opportunities that fail to support changes that would benefit a broader section of our community.”

One of the greatest challenges highlighted is the existing cultural belief around Australians wanting to own their own parcel of land and homes.

This is resulting in an urban sprawl that fails to create supportive, open communities that share spaces and foster the benefits of social interaction and social capital which contributes to a healthier, more fulfilling lifestyle.

Inclusive design is about far more than accessibility – it is about creating homes, buildings and public spaces that enable people of all ages, abilities and backgrounds to participate fully in community life.

The issue is how to move beyond designing spaces that people can access, to designing places where people genuinely feel they belong.

Consideration of neuro-inclusive design creates physical, digital, and social environments that accommodate diverse cognitive and sensory processing patterns, such as autism, ADHD, and dyslexia, benefiting roughly 15 percent to 20 percent of the population

Case studies have shown that those with these conditions benefit greatly from being immersed in the outdoors and connecting with the natural environment rather than being confined indoors.

The panel highlighted the benefits of planning ahead when designing a home so that it can cater for all ages and stages in life.

What also became apparent was the need for connected communities yet at the same time developments that offered a variety of housing designs and styles.

The connection is through workable streets and pathways to parks, recreation areas and shopping centres – good public transport, bikeways and footpaths rather than the straight line or grid pattern leading to urban sprawl.

The variety of housing comes after creative thinking rather than the cheapest option.

Well-designed density allows a community that shares and belongs to the public realm, John Mainwaring said.

It’s a matter of trying to get people to live in areas where it allows that integration of the public realm as well as the balance that coexists with the natural environment.

A lot of the medium density at Brightwater on the Sunshine Coast is built around a central water feature integrated with commercial development.

A pathway that runs all the way around the lake allows people to use it for recreation. It also allows residents to get in contact with the neighbourhood and engender a sense of community.

At the coastal Bokarina, where there is integrated living, people have a central shared green space, a foreshore reserve and access to the beach.

By eliminating front fences, the streets are being used as a public realm. The residents have realised they are able share the open space for recreation … share being the key word.

Unfortunately medium-density housing is being cut back in new residential developments due to the building boom and costs. It is not being seen as feasible to use social livability standards, even though they are embedded in the building code.

INCLUSION IS NOT ABOUT ASSUMING NEEDS OF OTHERS

Access is the means or opportunity to be able to approach or enter a place.

“Inclusivity is a topic we talk about a lot,” Cr Tina Kordrostami said, “but when it comes to neuro-diverse people and their lives we don’t see a lot of inclusion taking place.

“To make matters worse, up to 35 percent do not have access to employment or education, and up to 80 percent isolate at home.

“In sociology about 25 percent is needed for change to take place. … we have far exceeded that, keeping in mind many cannot have access to diagnosis.

“To help ensure this big portion can undertake everyday things we may take for granted, we need to start asking questions.

“In the design and building world we assume how someone’s house should look, how they should use that space, and who should be operating it.

“This is why we have people absconding from homes, and not feeling supported enough.

“A lot of disruption is taking place and it just doesn’t impact the neuro-diverse person, the individual themselves. It impacts everyone in the community that surrounds them.”

Cr Kordrostami suggested it was time to think about asking more questions and assuming less – after all, we are investing into our future.

It is important to help people understand that the more inclusive our environments are, the less we need to be putting in time, money and resources, and constantly changing the human perspective.

People are starting to realise how much is being lost by continually treating neuro-diversity as a checklist by people who assume everything and have no lived experience.

The environment can be the most impactful element of individual behavior. Case studies have shown that changing the environment can change behaviour.

A significant change can be made in regard to capacity building and the built design.

Capacity building is about moving on from maintaining an individual and allowing them to be independent.

Sharing a home with another participant can bring change due to the the sense of ownership and restablished family relationships.

Design can change and evolve, Cr Kordrostami said. Sensory-friendly design is common these days but more needs to be done.

Busy, noisy living rooms should see spaces of relief in every part of a house.

It’s the same as a public space, such as a library. It allows a person to self-regulate, have a moment of relief. Then, instead of isolating, they can re-enter the space they were in.

This inner self will allow them to build on their capacity.

Look at it as an in investment. The more people we have contributing to our society, the better off we all are.

We reduce challenging behaviors – less cases of absconding, vandalism and property damage.

Cr Kordrostami said it was heartbreaking to see the level of people self-isolating at home. as they have so much potential.

“Architecture is not everything , but it can impact life.

“Access is not just the ability to enter a space, but something in which to participate in – not just walk through.”

item.title: Zonta Walk Against Violence
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: From wearing orange and starting a conversation to planting a tree as a symbol of hope, every action sends a […]
item.content:encoded:
From wearing orange and starting a conversation to planting a tree as a symbol of hope, every action sends a powerful message during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence.

Held from 25 November to 10 December each year, the global movement shines a light on gender-based violence and encourages people everywhere to be part of the solution.

This year’s theme, UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity, highlights the importance of accountability, inclusion and lasting change.

Events held across the region include the Zonta Club of Noosa Walk Against Violence on 29 November, 8.30am, Lions Park Amphitheatre, Noosaville.

Other free community events include Service of Lament, 25 November, 10am, St Mark’s Anglican Church, Buderim, Rotary Pacific and Speak Up Now Walk Against Violence, 27 November, 9.30am, Tesch Park, Maleny and Seeds of Hope tree planting, 1 December, 7–9am, Alan Walker Park, Buddina.

In addition Zonta clubs from the Blackall Range, Caloundra, Maroochy and Noosa clubs are partnering in the Raise a Cup coffee sleeve initiative.

Throughout the 16 Days of Activism period, more than 30 local cafés will distribute takeaway coffee cups featuring campaign messages and information designed to raise awareness and connect people with support services.

Zonta Caloundra President Kathy Grudzinskas said the initiative helps to keep an important issue front of mind across the region.

“Through Raise a Cup, we’re taking an important message into places where people connect every day,” Ms Grudzinskas said.

“The 16 Days of Activism initiative reminds us that violence against women and girls is never acceptable, and that awareness is an important step towards change.

“We encourage Sunshine Coast residents to support local organisations involved in the campaign and help amplify the message across our community.”

Other organisations supporting activities throughout the Sunshine Coast include Centacare, DV Safe Phone, IFYS and the Sunshine Coast Domestic and Family Violence Co-ordination Service, alongside community groups, advocates and volunteers working to promote the cause.

The 16 Days of Activism movement is not only about raising awareness. It is also about supporting those impacted by violence and helping connect people with the information, services and assistance they may need.

To learn more about support services available, visit the webpages of Noosa and Sunshine Coast councils.

item.title: Council releases its Annual Report
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Preserving Noosa’s quality of life and environment are key drivers of the projects highlighted in Noosa Council’s 2025-2026 Annual Report. […]
item.content:encoded:
Preserving Noosa’s quality of life and environment are key drivers of the projects highlighted in Noosa Council’s 2025-2026 Annual Report.

Essential infrastructure, affordable housing investment, waste and recycling improvements and the distribution of more than $258,000 in community grants to support community events are among the details in the extensive, publicly available report.

Adopted by Council last week, the report outlines a year of significant investment in essential infrastructure, environmental protection, community facilities and services that support Noosa’s lifestyle and liveability.

A $51 million capital works program delivered upgrades and renewals across the shire, including $17.4 million invested in roads, bridges and transport infrastructure.

Key projects of the year included planning and design for the major upgrade of Doonella Lake Bridge – a project now nearing completion and expected to extend the life of the vital link between Tewantin and Noosaville by around 50 years.

Council also invested $10.3 million in waste and recycling improvements, $5.6 million in community facilities and sports grounds, and $6.3 million in pathways, parks, playgrounds, trail networks and public amenities. $5.2 million was spent on road reseals, $1 million in pathway renewals and $86,000 for the Sunshine Beach Skate Park renewal.

Mayor Frank Wilkie said the annual report reflected Council’s commitment to delivering results for the community while planning for Noosa’s future.

“The achievements outlined in this report reflect the dedication and professionalism of our CEO, directors and entire Council staff, whose commitment continues to make a positive difference across Noosa,” Mayor Wilkie said.

“Endorsement of the new 10-year Destination Management Plan to help protect Noosa’s lifestyle, natural environment and prosperity in the lead-up to the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games and beyond is another milestone of 2025-26.”

Affordable housing remained a key focus, with Council continuing its investment in facilitating development of 25 affordable dwellings at Lake Macdonald Drive for local families, young people and seniors on the Queensland Social Housing Register.

During the year, site remediation works were completed and $4.1 million secured from the Queensland Government’s Residential Activation Fund.

Council’s CEO Larry Sengstock said the report highlighted progress across a broad range of priorities.

“Council distributed more than $258,000 through Community Grants to support local events, projects and infrastructure, alongside almost $84,000 in Environment and Climate Change Response Grants that helped deliver positive sustainability outcomes across our community,” Mr Sengstock said.

The year also saw Council secure a 121-hectare conservation property at Kin Kin through the Environment Levy, advance accessibility with a new Changing Places facility at Gympie Terrace, complete community consultation on the Draft Noosa Botanic Gardens Master Plan and commission the Noosaville Community Battery, supporting a cleaner and more resilient energy future.

Customer service remained a key priority, with average phone wait times improving from 32 seconds to 29 seconds – well below the target maximum of 60 seconds.

The full 2025-2026 Annual Report is available on Council’s website.

item.title: Jones lands Supercars drive
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Sunshine Coast driver Harri Jones, 27, will make his full-time Supercars debut in 2027 after signing with Team 18. Jones […]
item.content:encoded:
Sunshine Coast driver Harri Jones, 27, will make his full-time Supercars debut in 2027 after signing with Team 18.

Jones will drive the Snowy River Racing Chevrolet Camaro alongside established race winner Anton De Pasquale, succeeding David Reynolds and completing Team 18’s full-time line-up for 2027.

It’s a return to familiar surroundings. Jones partnered De Pasquale in Team 18’s 2025 endurance campaign, scoring a top-ten finish on his Supercars debut at The Bend. This year he co-drove with Jack Le Brocq at Matt Stone Racing, finishing 10th at The Bend and fourth in the Bathurst 1000.

“To be returning to Team 18 as a full-time Supercars driver is an incredible opportunity and something I’ve worked towards for a long time,” Jones said.

“Coming back knowing the people and how the team operates gives me a good starting point. There will still be plenty to learn, but having Anton alongside me again is a huge benefit.”

Team 18 owner Charlie Schwerkolt said the team had seen Jones’ potential first-hand. “His continued success in Carrera Cup has reinforced our belief in what he can bring to the team,” Schwerkolt said.

Born and raised on the Coast and a graduate of Immanuel Lutheran College, Jones has carried the region’s name around the world, competing in the Porsche Supercup in Europe before returning home. He is now a three-time Porsche Carrera Cup Australia champion.

For all his success at national and international level, Jones remains firmly rooted on the Sunshine Coast. He is the founder of Jones Motor Culture, a Kunda Park workshop specialising in the service, storage and restoration of Porsche and other European marques. From the same workshop he runs his own Porsche Sprint Challenge team, Jones Motorsport, which develops and mentors the next generation of Australian racing talent.

“I never came through karting, so to be lining up on the Supercars grid full-time is something special. I hope it shows young people on the Coast that the path is there if you’re prepared to work for it,” Jones said.

“I couldn’t have done it without the Sunshine Coast businesses and individuals who have backed me every step of the way, and I’m proud to be taking the Coast with me into 2027.”

Further details of Jones’ preparations and Team 18’s 2027 season will be announced in due course. Fans can follow Harri’s road to his first full-time Supercars season on Instagram at @harrijones99, and keep up with the workshop at @jonesmotorculture.

item.title: Can playing music help keep you young?
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Noosa is renowned for its enviable lifestyle and its health-conscious population. Many residents enjoy the advantage of having both the […]
item.content:encoded:
Noosa is renowned for its enviable lifestyle and its health-conscious population. Many residents enjoy the advantage of having both the time and financial means to invest in their health, wellbeing and personal interests. As people look for ways to stay active, mentally stimulated and socially connected as they get older, learning a musical instrument offers a particularly rewarding opportunity.

Playing music is much more than an enjoyable pastime. Scientific research increasingly demonstrates the benefits of musical learning for the ageing brain. A 2024 academic research paper published in Brain and Cognition Journal involving over 500 older adults found that learning an instrument can improve aspects of mental processing speed, concentration and cognitive flexibility.

Learning an instrument engages multiple areas of the brain simultaneously. Remembering chords, coordinating fingers, listening and developing new skills provide a stimulating mental workout. It can also improve dexterity, encourage creativity, reduce stress and provide a genuine sense of achievement.

Learning an instrument with an experienced teacher brings further benefits. At Music at Noosa, teachers tailor lessons to each student’s abilities, interests and pace of learning. Lessons provide motivation, encouragement and the satisfaction of mastering something new.

Importantly, music brings people together. Lessons, group activities and playing with others create opportunities for friendships, social interaction and a sense of belonging.

Invest in yourself. Keep your mind active. Make new friends. Discover the lifelong pleasure of making music.

It’s never too late to start!

item.title: ZEN recognised in Biosphere Awards
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Zero Emissions Noosa’s Business Energy Advisor program won the Smart Biosphere Award at the 2026 Noosa Biosphere Awards on Thursday […]
item.content:encoded:
Zero Emissions Noosa’s Business Energy Advisor program won the Smart Biosphere Award at the 2026 Noosa Biosphere Awards on Thursday 12 November.

Noosa’s Business Energy Advisor program helps businesses to reduce their energy use and costs, while reducing their carbon footprint. That is smart business.

Noosa’s small businesses face rising energy bills, a confusing and changing energy market, and limited opportunity to get straightforward, unbiased advice. Most owners know they could save but they lack the time, trust, and information to act.

The Business Energy Advisor program fills that gap, offering free, independent and local advice for businesses to save money and emissions.

Zero Emissions Noosa (ZEN) has run the program since September 2025, proudly supported by Noosa Shire Council. Attending local business events, the Advisor makes 1-on-1 contact with business owners and meets them on their terms.

Since then, the Advisor has visited 59 businesses. Projects installed or contracted so far will save local businesses $121k+ a year, boosting their value proposition and business resilience. The combination of installed and contracted projects will cut 392+ tonnes of CO2-e each year, while boosting business resilience via solar and battery installations and helping community decarbonisation via EV chargers.

Local businesses will save $1,216,852 over ten years with 3,926 tonnes of CO2-e saved,

The program supports three UNESCO Man and the Biosphere objectives, helping businesses work within the Noosa Biosphere.

Climate: new and repaired solar avoids 115 tonnes of emissions a year, and batteries keep businesses open in blackouts.

Sustainable development: savings stay in local businesses and install work goes to local trades.

Learning: the advisor met owners at 33 business events and shares results through case study videos and articles.

Mayan Farm Villas, one of the Business Energy Advisor’s clients, was joint winner of the Sustainable Business Award. They are now blackout proof and making big energy bill savings after installing solar, batteries and an EV Charger. Congratulations to Jodie & the team.

The Business Energy Advisor program continues to go from strength to strength with potential for further savings. If you are a business owner who wants to know more about how to save on your energy bill, reach out to Josh at josh.stevens@zeroemissionsnoosa.com

Zero Emissions Noosa Inc. (ZEN) was also a proud finalist in the Biosphere Social Impact Award for the Noosa E Bike Library.

The first of its kind in Queensland, it lets residents test, free, five different types of ebikes for 2 week loans, with home delivery and pick-up.

Jenny Clement, E Bike Library Project Leader says, “Once people have tried an ebike they are much more likely to buy their own. 87% of survey respondents say they have or plan to buy their own ebike after the loan.”

E bikes are a perfect solution for swapping out short car trips. Cycling has proven health and mental well-being benefits. E cycling reduces emissions and traffic congestion – contributing to a more environmentally friendly Noosa, helping residents to live in our Biosphere.

Jenny says, “The initiative also has social benefits. Several customers have health or physical reasons for wanting to ride ebikes, so they can get out to shops and clubs, helping them overcome social isolation.”

Feedback from satisfied clients includes, “It’s been absolutely wonderful. I’ve actually decided to buy one because I felt that it was replacing all those little car trips”.

ZEN’s Noosa eBike Library is proudly supported by Noosa Council and is implemented in collaboration with a local ebike company, ecoTekk. To try an E bike, zeroemissionsnoosa.com.au/project/noosa-e-bike-library/#form

item.title: Slavery, safety and saris
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Slave trafficking of women and girls – some as young as 10 – in Bangalore, India, is a long way […]
item.content:encoded:
Slave trafficking of women and girls – some as young as 10 – in Bangalore, India, is a long way from the Sunshine Beach Anglican Church’s Christmas Market fundraiser on Saturday 28 November.

For the church’s office administrator Priya Kirubakaran, however, the connection is very real and a feature of the market will be tote and other utility bags made from pre-loved saris by the rescued women that she has donated.

A computer science specialist Priya was in Bangalore for 18 months recently and wanted to work for a non-profit organisation while she was there.

“I chose Freedom Project India which operates a safe house providing shelter, care, and dignity to women and children who are survivors of human trafficking and exploitation.

“It was devastating to hear their stories, to learn what the girls had been through but it was also heartening to see them building skills like artisan craft training, making handcrafted bags and wellness products like natural soap. There is a lovely lady who is a tailor and she has trained the girls to make the different types of bags.

“I wanted to make a contribution so I bought the bags before I left and I have given them to the church.”

Coordinator of the Market is church member, Dr Anne Jobling, who is Honorary Researcher in Disability at UQ. She told Noosa Today money raised from the fundraiser would be given to the support the work of Chaplain Simone Weaver at Sunshine Beach State Primary and Kimberly King at Sunshine Beach High.

“The Chappies are so vital for the wellbeing and emotional support of students. They are there for the disadvantaged, for children who are hungry, the homeless and those in need in times of crisis.

She said as well as the bags other bargains for sale would be baking, jams, plants, specialist china and glassware, books and jewellery.

“We are very grateful for the contributions by Priya and all our other supporters.

Christmas Market, St Andrews Church Bicentennial Drive Sunshine Beach, Saturday 28 November, 9am-3pm.

Sizzle and Sounds

Get your friends together, bring a chair and relax by the Noosa River, 2-5pm on Saturday 28 November on the lawn in front of the Noosa Yacht & Rowing Club. The Kombi Van will be serving Squealing Pig wines, can bar available and live music with Maurice Milani. Games, promotional giveaways and a free sausage sizzle.

Tewantin-Noosa RSL Women’s Auxiliary

The final meeting of the Year & our Christmas Lunch will be held on Friday 4 December, with our meeting at 10-30am followed by our Christmas Lunch in the Dining Room.

Cost; $20 members $25 non members. Please bring a gift (unwrapped) for the Salvation Army children’s xmas appeal. Please Ph; Kay 0402804270 to book.

Sea Scouts Fundraiser

This Christmas, buy your real tree from Noosa Sea Scouts and support the youth in our community. Scouting provides young people with opportunities to develop valuable life skills, confidence and teamwork through adventure, outdoor activities and new experiences.

Pre-order your real Christmas tree online at noosascoutxmastrees.com by Friday 27 November. Choose from two collection dates, Saturday 28 November or Saturday 5 December, with delivery also available.

Talks program

U3A noosa Friday Talks are held at 1.30 pm at U3A, 64 Poinciana Ave. Tewantin

Friday 20 November 2026 Darrel Roche – Somerset.

Friday 27 November 2026 Zero Emissions Noosa – Swap the Drive: Can We Make Noosa More Liveable?

Full details available on U3A website www.u3anoosa.com.au/

SUNSHINE COAST PARKINSON’S ACTIVITY GROUP

The Sunshine Coast Parkinson’s Activity Group meets at 10.30am on the third Friday of each month at the Noosa Tewantin Bowls Club, Hilton Tce, Tewantin. The group welcomes people living with Parkinson’s disease and other neurological disorders, as well as their carers, family members, and supporters.

Meetings provide an opportunity to share information, discuss relevant issues and enjoy the support of others. Learn about new developments in Parkinson’s research and things that will help you in your journey.

Guided activities are also available to people with Parkinson’s disease, restricted movement, or voice difficulties. You do not need to be a member of the group to participate.

For further information, contact Kaye on 0428 201 178.

HOST INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS

Sunshine Beach State High School is seeking local families to host international students for six months from January 2027. All you need is a spare room, a welcoming home, and meals for your student. Generous financial reimbursement and ongoing support provided. Interested? phone Sharon Forbes on 54404294 or email sforb23@eq.edu.au

BOTANIC GARDENS NEEDS VOLUNTEERS

The Friends of Noosa Botanic Gardens are on the lookout for enthusiastic volunteers to help maintain our beautiful gardens, learn more about gardening, meet new friends and welcome visitors. If you can spare a few hours on a Thursday morning, your contribution will be greatly valued and appreciated. No prior experience needed – just a positive attitude and willingness to lend a hand. If you’re keen to join us, contact Julie Bartlett (0416 225941) or Willy Ostwald (0417 332787) for a chat.

NORTH TEWANTIN BUSHCARE

Join the North Tewantin Bush Care Group of local volunteers every first and third Sunday of the month from 7.30-9.30am to help maintain the beautiful natural flora in the area. We weed & plant along the river. It is light work and a lot of fun. All equipment is provided and an excellent morning tea follows. Grab a hat and come along. Phone 0432384596.

BOOMERANG BAGS NOOSA

Fabric donations always needed. Boomerang bags are sewn from recycled fabric with the aim of reducing single use plastic bags and minimising landfill from discarded textiles. Any unwanted fabric: doona covers, sheets, denim, curtains or upholstery fabric can be dropped off at Wallace House on a Monday or Wednesday morning. Phone Ned: 0411 784 911. Facebook: boomerangbagsnoosa

CROQUET CLUB

Free ‘Come & Try’ Croquet every Sunday at 08.15am at Noosa Croquet Club 9 Seashell Place, Noosaville. Phone Ed 0402 246 833 or Bob 0421 041 021.

SUNDAY DANCE

Every Sunday, from 12.30pm at the Tewantin Masonic Hall, Moorindil St. We start by teaching basic dance steps, then Waltz, old time, New Vogue, Ballroom Dances and a little Latin. We run to 5pm. Lots of fun and dancing, including a 20 min. tea/coffee break to socialise. (Only $10) Hope to see you there. Guys needed, so men, free lessons for the first six weeks. Singles or couples welcome. Just rock up or phone Andrew 0429 829 328. For more info, please visit andrewsclassdance.com

THE GLORY OF OPERA

Enjoy the music and the artistry of opera live on screen at U3A auditorium at Tewantin with tutor and opera buff Jeremy Martin. Starting at 9.30am on Mondays, Jeremy, using online documentaries, explores the lives and careers of celebrated present and past composers, conductors and singers. We encourage discussion and we have a lot of fun. New members are always welcome and you don’t have to be an opera lover to join. Contact Jeremy on 0406 959 097 or jdm@kaput.com

VIEW CLUB

The Noosaville VIEW Club is a valued part of The Smith Family dedicated to supporting the education and wellbeing of disadvantaged Australian children. On the 2nd Thursday of each month this warm and welcoming women’s club gathers for our “Friendship Day” nosh and camaraderie. On the 4th Thursday of each month we have our club lunch meeting at the Tewantin RSL with a guest speaker and update on our fourteen Learning for Life students. New members and guests are always welcome to come along for fun and friendship.

For more information email viewnoosaville@gmail.com

SENIORS INDOOR BOWLS

If you are interested in a low impact, friendly activity then indoor bowls is for you. We are a group of seniors enjoying the health benefits of interacting with like minded and friendly people. Experience is not necessary and a high standard is not expected. The aim is fun and friendship. We meet every Friday at the Noosa Leisure Centre in Wallace Drive. Arrival time is between 8.30 and 8.45 for a 9am start. Pop in to see how it works or ring me (Pam) on 0407 493 402.

MAGZ JAZZ

Increase strength, flexibility, energy and wellbeing. Dance exercises and stretch. Learn new dance moves and routines to inspired music. Jazz & Latin style dance keeps body moving, mind agile, memory working and spirit lifted. Tuesdays 8am-9.30am in Tewantin. Phone Margaret for details 0425 269 988

JOIN ZONTA CLUB OF NOOSA

For over 30 years, the Zonta Club of Noosa -proudly affiliated with Zonta International – has strived to empower local women through education bursaries, and health initiatives, providing advocacy and support for issues caused by gender-based violence and homelessness. We host fundraising and advocacy events throughout the year. Join us for our monthly dinner meetings.

Visit zontanoosa.org or email admin@zontanoosa.org

HERE’S A NOVEL IDEA

So you want to write a best-seller? Or perhaps you’ve had the idea of a story rattling around your brain forever. If that’s the case, bring your novel ideas or part-written fiction and join us at Noosa Novelists at our meetings on Monday mornings at Wallace House, Noosa, when we read and comment on pre-emailed chapters of each other’s work, offering ideas and suggestions in friendly discussion to help develop our stories. If interested, please email Noosa Shire Arts and Crafts at create@noosaartsandcrafts.org.au and head it ‘Novelists enquiry.’ Please give details of any publications past and present, or work in progress.

COMMUNITY GARDEN

New Members welcomed. We can offer memberships for fit and active individuals, who are eager to participate in our organic vegetable, herb and fruit garden activities on Friday mornings in Noosaville. Call 0416 054 650.

THURSDAY GIRLS

The Thursday Girls is a registered Australian charity, run by a committee of volunteers. We are a group of women who are passionate about supporting children whose families are suffering financial hardship. Local schools apply to The Thursday Girls for grants for individual students. If the application is successful, The Thursday Girls will transfer funds directly to the school to provide the nominated student access to new opportunities and educational resources, such as a school camp or new sports or educational equipment. The committee arranges monthly fundraising lunches (and other events) at local restaurants. Join us and meet others or get your friends together. Contact: Linn 0418 103 008

AUSTRALIAN MOTORHOMING LIONS CLUB

Are you passionate about giving back and supporting the amazing charitable work that Lions Clubs accomplish across Australia? The Australian Motorhoming Lions Club is looking for new members from all walks of life—no camping vehicle required! As a travelling club, we assist other Lions clubs with their projects as we journey from place to place, raising funds and lending a helping hand wherever we go. Join us now, for further information please contact us via email: membership@amlc.org.au, or phone Lynne 0408 366 299

SENIORS SOCIAL GROUP

We welcome singles and couples to join us for coffee and conversation in a warm, friendly atmosphere, with no joining fees, at the Boathouse on the Noosa River, Thursdays, 10am as well as Tuesdays at the Tewantin Marina Wine bar, 10 am. We also have other optional social activities including lunches, dinners, trivia, picnics, live music events etc. Please call Joan on 0419517869 for more information.

CAN LAUGH

We are a small group who meet once a month. We started some years ago as a Breast Cancer Support Group, but over the years we have people who came with other forms of cancer for support, so if you would like to come and have a chat with us we would love to say hello. We meet the first Friday of the month at the CWA Hall, Tewantin 10am to 12noon. Phone Val: 0422 997 781 or 0427 868 163.

GUILDED LILIES

The Guilded Lilies meet on the last Saturday of every month at the Masonic Hall, Moorindal St, Tewantin, 9am-3pm. Come along, meet new friends, learn new skills, enjoy the company of like minded people. All crafts welcome. Phone Angela 0408 068 148

SALVOS MATES SUPPORT

Phone us about our new men’s mental health support group. You may be interested as a bloke who would like a private chat about your wellbeing? Or you have a friend in need? We (SMS) are an all-male group, typically outdoor type retirees. If you are interested as a volunteer, we are particularly looking for men living in the regional towns such as Cooroy, Pomona, Eumundi. Phone Mike, Al, or Peter on 0423 317 375.

NOOSA DAYBREAK ROTARY

If you’ve had a fulfilling career and are interested in ’Giving Back’ to the community, join us at Noosa Marina, Café VinCino. We meet every Thursday at 7:30am for about an hour or so, and breakfast. We are a group of around 24 people who live in and around Noosa. We raise funds and support organizations that assist people in our community. Our current major project, in partnership with the Salvation Army’s ‘First Response Team,’ is helping the homeless transition from sleeping in their cars to leading a normal life. Come and have a chat with us.

NATIONAL SENIORS

Tewantin Noosa National Seniors group meet at Tewantin RSL on the third Thursday of each month at 10.30am. We offer outings, social gatherings, information sharing and friendship. Morning tea is served and we have guest speakers each month who share valuable information with our members. We welcome new members and visitors are also welcome to these meetings. For more information about our group please contact president Colleen Riley 0417 849 473.

BOOK CLUB WITH A TWIST

We are a small and friendly group of adults who like talking and/or listening to discussions about books, authors, illustrators, characters and word choices. There is no prescribed reading that you have to do (that’s the twist!). Just bring along any book that you have read, or are currently reading, to discuss informally. All book genres are welcome. Everyone is welcome. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month at the tables inside Cooroy Library 1pm – 2ish. Completely free. Email contact is bookclubwithatwist@hotmail.com

PROBUS CLUBS

Probus Clubs are designed for fun and friendship in retirement. If you are retired (or nearly) and are open to making new friends through a variety of activities, then Noosa has several Probus clubs.

PROBUS 2010

Noosa Probus 2010 is a great club for retired men and women who love going on bus trips, having coffee, lunches, dinners, weekly walks, yoga, theatre, garden outings and more. Meetings are held at Lawns (Tewantin Noosa Bowls Club) 65 Hilton Tce, Tewantin on the second Tuesday of the month at 9am. Enquiries Win 0481 397 272.

VEGGIE VILLAGE

Veggie Village at Rufous St Peregian Beach is a community garden growing organic fruit, herbs and vegetables. Membership is open to anyone who wants to learn more about gardening, share their knowledge or just make some friends. Veggie Village has individual plots for rent plus communal plots that we look after and share. Contact us on info@veggievillage.org.au or visit veggievillage.org.au

ACTIVITY WITH PARKINSONS

The Parkinsons Activity Group, provides activities for Parkinsons sufferers, the activities range from Boxercise in the Box Office, 25 Project Avenue (0422 485 482) Georgina, Physio-led exercise (0490 444 255) Emily, Speech Therapy voice and choir (0400 037 901) Edwina. Call Ann for an info pamphlett on 0458 009 601. Parkinsons Group meets the third Friday of each month at Noosa Tewantin Bowls Club at 10.30am for information and lunch. You need to stay active and socialise to help deal with the symptoms.

FABULOUS 60S PLUS

We are a fun, friendly, seniors social group. We welcome couples and singles to join us for morning coffee every Tuesday at the Noosa Marina wine bar Tewantin, from 10am and every Thursday at the Boathouse on the Noosa River from 10 am. We also have a monthly program of lunches, dinners, picnics, walks and other fun activities. Contact Joan on 0419 517 869 for more details.

PHOTO CLUB

We meet on the second Monday of each month at Uniting Church Hall, 6 Grasstree Court, Sunrise Beach at 7pm. The club comprises all levels of expertise form novice to professional. The night comprises a guest speaker, supper and our monthly critique of member’s work. Visitors welcome.

BEEF AND BURGUNDY CLUB

Noosa Beefsteak and Burgundy club meet on the third Wednesday evening of the month at a different local restaurant for good food, wine and fellowship. We invite couples or singles to join us. Further information contact John Dicker on 0414 323 266.

FAMILY HISTORY

The Heritage Centre at 17 Emerald Street in Cooroy welcomes visitors to research family and local history. Volunteers are there to help.

Access a wide range of resources including a library, computers, digital databases and subscriptions to MyHeritage, Ancestry.com, FindmyPast and more.

Open Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays 9.30am-1pm Information ph. 07 3129 0356 or visit genealogy-noosa.org.au

MENS SHED

The Noosa Men’s Shed provides a venue for the men of Noosa to gather in an environment of traditional Australian mateship. It aims to advance the health, well being and social inclusion based on individual interests of the members. The Shed also offers facilities and support for many activities: woodwork, metalwork, gardening, arts studio, music, hobbies (leatherwork, technology, amateur radio), health and wellbeing, bee keeping, aquaponics and hydroponics. Membership is $120 per year. Visit the Shed office on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 8-11am at Rotary Lane off Wallum Lane, Noosa Springs.

TOASTMASTERS

We are a supportive public speaking club dedicated to improving your confidence and creativity in a safe environment. Our meetings are every 2nd and 4th Monday of the month, from 6.30-8.30pm at the CWA Hall, Tewantin. The first two visits are free. For more information email noosatoastmasters@gmail.com

TUNE IN TO NOOSA FM

Tune in Noosa FM 101.3 or stream live on noosafm.org for local updates and Great Music for a Great Community. Noosa’s community radio station is committed to developing local talent
